content: Since the advent of in-vitro fertilization (IVF), surgical interventions on the fallopian tubes have become less common as a method to address infertility in women with tubal damage. However, various surgical techniques are available to repair blocked or damaged fallopian tubes. This study aimed to assess the role of tubal surgery in managing tubal infertility and to evaluate specific surgical techniques used for this purpose. The review utilized a search strategy developed by the Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group. Relevant trials were identified from the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group Specialised Register and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL). Additional searches were conducted using the OVID platform in databases such as MEDLINE (1966 to July 2005) and EMBASE (1980 to July 2005). The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the following topics related to infertility surgery: 1. The role of infertility surgery compared to no treatment. 2. The role of infertility surgery compared to alternative treatments. 3. The role of magnification in surgical procedures. 4. The use of CO2 lasers in infertility surgery. 5. The role of operative laparoscopy in performing infertility surgery. 6. Any other surgical interventions studied in RCTs. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors, and any disagreements were resolved through consensus. For each trial, two-by-two tables were generated to analyze the dichotomous outcome of pregnancy. The effects on pregnancy rates were expressed as odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Seven randomized controlled trials were identified. However, no RCTs were found that compared infertility surgery to no treatment or alternative treatments. Additionally, no RCTs investigated the use of magnification in tubal surgery. Regarding the use of CO2 lasers, two RCTs provided no evidence of benefit or disadvantage when compared to standard techniques for adhesiolysis (OR for pregnancy 1.07, 95% CI 0.40 to 2.87) or salpingostomy (OR for pregnancy 1.38, 95% CI 0.47 to 4.05). One RCT compared salpingostomatolysis performed via laparotomy versus laparoscopy, using either the classic approach or the one-suture technique. No evidence of benefit or disadvantage was found when laparoscopy was compared to laparotomy. The OR for bilateral tubal patency was 1.32 (95% CI 0.55 to 3.22), and for unilateral tubal patency, the OR was 0.82 (95% CI 0.29 to 2.29). Pregnancy rates were not reported in this study. Two RCTs assessed the use of a prosthesis during salpingostomy compared to non-use. There was no evidence of benefit or disadvantage, with the combined OR for pregnancy at term being 1.17 (95% CI 0.47 to 2.93). One RCT compared the Cuff technique to the Bruhat technique for salpingostomy and found no evidence of benefit or disadvantage. Another RCT compared two methods of salpingostomy, reporting an OR for intrauterine pregnancy of 1.02 (95% CI 0.22 to 4.61). One RCT evaluated the use of thermocoagulation versus electrocoagulation during adhesiolysis. No evidence of benefit or disadvantage was found, with the OR for pregnancy rates between the two groups being 0.87 (95% CI 0.51 to 1.46). In conclusion, the limited data available do not provide evidence of benefit or disadvantage for tubal surgery compared to no treatment or alternative treatments. Similarly, there is no evidence to suggest an advantage or disadvantage of using microsurgery over standard techniques, laparoscopy over laparotomy, CO2 lasers, or electrocoagulation over thermocoagulation. Further randomized controlled trials are necessary to determine the role of tubal surgery compared to no treatment or alternative treatments, as well as the role of specific techniques such as magnification, laparoscopy, lasers, or electrocoagulation in tubal surgery.
